title: Viecier, i sokał, i ja…
poem:
I viecier, i sokał, i ja —
Syny adnoj doli-žyccia,
Navodzim markotnyja my
I dumy, i piesni adny.

Razniaŭ viecier krylli svaje,
Lacić, i šumić, i piaje;
Piaje a svabodzie svajej,
Piaje a niavoli ludziej.

Jak viecier, i ja b tak lacieŭ,
Jak viecier, ab tym samym pieŭ,
Jak viecier, svabodny moj duch,
Choć ruki zakuty ŭ łancuh.

Pad zorami sokał zavis,
Hladzić pa-arlinamu ŭniz.
Tam sokału svietu nie žal;
Milej jamu niebnaja dal.

Jak sokał, i ja b mknuŭ da zor:
Tam sonca, razdolle, prastor;
Biez žalu b pakinuŭ ziamlu,
I chatku, i dolu svaju.

I viecier, i sokał, i ja —
Syny adnoj doli-žyccia;
Navodzim markotnyja my
I dumy, i piesni adny.
poem_note: Modern łacinka transcription. Source: Belarusian Palichka, knihi.com; collected works, vol. 1 (1995). [12]

title: Your reading path
paragraphs: An English-language companion to traditional Belarusian łacinka: ł/l, v, č, š, ž and ŭ. Belarusian examples keep their language; changing scripts does not automatically change spelling. This is not a passport romanization guide.
Start with the alphabet and try the exercises. Then return to the historical pages and poetry. Page numbers include the cover.
Six separate watercolor pages tell the stork's story: 4, 9, 16, 21, 27 and 32. This is an illustrated thread, not an account of the history of the alphabet.
callout:
A different script. The same language.
бусел / busieł / stork

title: Who invented it?
paragraphs: No single established inventor can be named. Belarusian łacinka developed as a tradition of writing Belarusian in Latin letters, rather than as one person's invention on one particular date. [1, 2]

Early surviving examples are associated with the late sixteenth century. In the seventeenth century, Belarusian dialogue was recorded in Latin script, including theatrical interludes. Polish graphic conventions strongly influenced early practice. [1]

During the nineteenth century, łacinka became an important vehicle for modern Belarusian literature. Letters and spelling conventions continued to change; today's chart cannot simply be imposed on every old edition. [1, 2]
callout: Ask who wrote, printed, circulated and codified it.

title: Writers and books
paragraphs: Vincient Dunin-Marcinkievič: his Belarusian translation of the first two books of Pan Tadeusz appeared in Vilnius in 1859 in Latin script and was confiscated. This was the Belarusian translation, not Mickiewicz's Polish original. [1, 6]
Francišak Bahuševič: Dudka biełaruskaja appeared in Kraków in 1891 under the name Maciej Buračok. Smyk biełaruski followed in 1894 under Symon Reŭka z-pad Barysava. Both were printed in łacinka. [5]
Kastuś Kalinoŭski: editor and one of the authors of Mužyckaja praŭda (1862-1863), a newspaper printed in Latin script. His role here is chiefly that of publicist and editor. [7]
callout: An author, an editor and a codifier play different roles.

title: Readers and reformers
paragraphs: Ciotka (Ałaiza Paškievič): the publisher's advertisement in Kupala's Žalejka (1908) lists her primer alongside a Cyrillic edition. Its title in a modern łacinka reading is Pieršaje čytańnie dla dzietak biełarusaŭ; this is not a diplomatic transcription of the advertisement. [6]

Janka Kupała: Huślar (1910) is a concrete example of his poetry in Latin script. This does not make every edition of his work Latin-script: the inspected Žalejka (1908) has a Cyrillic main text. [6, 8]
Branisłaŭ Taraškievič: his school grammar appeared in Vilnius in 1918 in both scripts. He codified an existing language and writing tradition; he did not invent łacinka from nothing. [4]
callout: A printed Latin edition is not automatically evidence of a Latin-script autograph.

title: Inside an old edition
paragraphs: These are reading clues, not universal correction rules. Historical editions differ in both graphic conventions and spelling. [2, 8]
Record the author, title, date and script. Compare recurring words before calling an unfamiliar spelling a mistake.
Keep two lines in your notes: 'as printed' and 'my modern rendering'. Never silently modernize a quotation.
callout:
Łacinka is a script tradition.
Taraškievica is an orthographic system.

title: Letters · A to K
rows: ґ · a stop, distinct from h
paragraphs: Correspondences: [2, 3]. Do not read e, c or j as English letters. The use of g for the separate stop sound depends on the word's orthographic treatment.
callout: г / h · х / ch · ґ / g

title: Letters · L to Ž
rows: Z z · Ź ź · Ž ž
paragraphs: Before a vowel, i may signal softness. The letter l is already soft. [2, 3]
callout: Remember: ł = л, but ŭ = ў.

title: Letters working together
paragraphs: Ch, dz and dž are stable combinations; šč represents a sequence of š + č. Dź marks softness. [2, 3]
Мядзьведзь is the classical spelling. Preserving modern мядзведзь gives miadzviedź instead. Keep the two source spellings distinct.
Read chata, džem and ščupak aloud; cover the examples and reconstruct their Cyrillic forms.
callout:
Caron: č, š, ž. Acute: ć, ń, ś, ź.
Breve: ŭ.

title: The cover letter: Ŭ
paragraphs: Latin Ŭ ŭ corresponds to Belarusian Ў ў. Its mark is a breve: a small curve, not a straight bar. The base letter is U, not Y. [2, 3]
Ў does not form a separate syllable. English w offers a rough starting point; listening to Belarusian speech is better. [3]
callout:
У / u and ў / ŭ are different.
Notice the letter in a complete word.

title: Ł and L
paragraphs: The last consonant in busieł is hard; in sol it is soft. Before i, soft л is written l. [2, 3]
After soft l, use a, e, o, u for я, е, ё, ю: ля / la, ле / le, лё / lo, лю / lu. Do not add an extra i mechanically.
If you know Polish, take special care: Belarusian ł here represents hard л, not the usual modern Polish pronunciation of ł.
callout: лес / les · лёд / lod · людзі / ludzi

title: Softness: acute or i?
paragraphs: At a word's end, an acute can mark softness: дзень / dzień, конь / koń, пісаць / pisać. There is no separate letter for ь. [2, 3]
Before a vowel, i usually does the work: ня / nia, ця / cia, ся / sia, зя / zia. Compare дзень / dzień with дня / dnia.
Do not add both an acute and i automatically. Check the consonant's position and the source spelling.
callout: L is already soft: соль / sol.

title: Choosing j or i
rows: я / ja · е / je · ё / jo · ю / ju
ня / nia · не / nie · нё / nio · ню / niu
ля / la · ле / le · лё / lo · лю / lu
paragraphs: A separate й before a vowel is written j. The apostrophe is therefore not copied mechanically: сям’я / siamja, аб’ява / abjava, надвор’е / nadvorje. [3]
Find the vowel, examine what precedes it, then check separately for l and for a distinct j sound.
callout:
яма / jama · мая / maja
няма / niama · лямпа / lampa

title: One script, several choices
paragraphs: Classical orthography marks assimilative softness in some positions where modern spelling does not. The difference may already exist in the Cyrillic source. [3, 4]
Choose a main approach for your notebook and label other spellings when quoting them.
Traditional łacinka is not identical to geographical romanization systems: its distinction between ł and l is one useful sign. [2, 9]
callout:
Choose the source spelling first.
Then choose the letters.

title: Words to keep
paragraphs: Copy five words, then add one of your own. Stress is not marked here. Apply the rules on pages 10-17.
callout:
A first line:
бусел / busieł · гняздо / hniazdo

title: A stork by the house
paragraphs: Раніца. Каля хаты стаіць дрэва. На дрэве гняздо. У гняздзе бусел. Я гляджу на птушку і пішу ў кнізе: «Добры дзень!»
Ranica. Kala chaty staić dreva. Na drevie hniazdo. U hniazdzie busieł. Ja hladžu na ptušku i pišu ŭ knizie: «Dobry dzień!»
Morning. A tree stands by the house. There is a nest in the tree and a stork in the nest. I look at the bird and write in the book: 'Good day!'
Original practice text, not a literary quotation. Find ch, dz, dž, soft l, ie and ŭ. Copy three words you recognized without the Cyrillic.
callout:
Why kala, but słova?
The л in каля is soft; in слова it is hard.

title: Try it yourself
paragraphs: 1. Write in łacinka: хата, бусел, гняздо, воўк, дзень, людзі.
2. Restore Cyrillic: mała, les, lod, dziakuj, vosień, pišu.
3. Insert ł or l: __uk (лук), __uk (люк), busie__ (бусел), so__ (соль).
4. Choose: яма - jama or iama? Няма - njama or niama? Мая - maja or maia?
5. Write two sentences about a bird or a book. Start in Cyrillic, then use łacinka. Check each soft consonant.
callout:
Answers are on page 24.
Try first without the chart.

title: Look a little closer
paragraphs: 6. Find the error: shata for хата; belarus for Беларусь; slova for слова.
7. Explain: u / ŭ; c / č; s / ś / š.
8. Write in łacinka: сям’я, надвор’е, я, ця, лёд.
9. Preserve each source spelling: снег; сьнег; песня; песьня.
10. An old edition uses sz and w. Must its language be Polish? How would you check?
callout: An unfamiliar spelling is an invitation to investigate.

title: Your answer key
paragraphs: 1. chata, busieł, hniazdo, voŭk, dzień, ludzi.
2. мала, лес, лёд, дзякуй, восень, пішу.
3. łuk; luk; busieł; sol.
4. jama; niama; maja.
5. One answer: Гэта кніга. Тут бусел. / Heta kniha. Tut busieł.
6. chata; Biełaruś; słova. Check х, ie, ł and final ś.
7. у / ў; ц / ч; с / сь / ш.
8. siamja, nadvorje, ja, cia, lod.
9. snieh; śnieh; piesnia; pieśnia.
10. No. These can be historical łacinka conventions. Check the language, title, date and edition.
callout: Name the rule, then make one new example.

title: Letters by hand
paragraphs: Write slowly: Ŭ ŭ · Ł ł · Ć ć · Ń ń · Ś ś · Ź ź · Č č · Š š · Ž ž.
Keep the curved breve, slanted acute and angled caron distinct. Do not let the stroke of ł disappear into a ruled line.
Then write busieł, hniazdo and Biełaruś. Add a date and a sentence of your own.
callout:
Date · subject · source
Leave room to change your mind.

title: Wind, falcon, and I
paragraphs: Вецер, і сокал, і я… / Viecier, i sokał, i ja…

This is the closest match to the book's theme: flight embodies a spirit that remains free despite constraint. The following excerpt follows the Cyrillic text in Kupala's collected works, volume 1 (1995), as presented by Belarusian Palichka. [12]

Як вецер, свабодны мой дух,
Хоць рукі закуты ў ланцуг.

Jak viecier, svabodny moj duch,
Choć ruki zakuty ŭ łancuh.
English sense: My spirit is free as the wind, though my hands are chained.
The łacinka here is our modern reading transcription, not a facsimile of an early edition. Other editions have a different second line; we do not mix them.
callout:
v ie c ie r · ŭ · ł
Notice ie, short ŭ and hard ł.

title: A prayer to the wind
paragraphs: Мая малітва / Maja malitva
Choose the poem beginning «Ва ўсяку мінуту…». Kupala wrote more than one poem with this title. This one addresses sun, wind, water, sky and the wider world. [13]

Малюся свабоднаму ветру—віхуры,
Што лётае птушкай ад краю да краю,

Malusia svabodnamu vietru—vichury,
Što lotaje ptuškaj ad kraju da kraju,
English sense: I pray to the free whirlwind, flying like a bird from one edge of the world to the other.

The Cyrillic excerpt follows the 1926 collected-edition text on Wikisource. The łacinka transcription and English sense are prepared for this reader; neither is presented as an original historical translation.
callout:
лётае / lotaje · птушкай / ptuškaj
After soft l, ё becomes o.

title: Freedom and open space
paragraphs: Сымон-музыка / Symon-muzyka
A longer narrative poem about a gifted musician. It offers a further reading path for the artist's longing for freedom and room to create. [14]
This edition provides a reading recommendation only. No passage from Kołas's poem, Latin-script transcription of a passage, or English translation of a passage is reproduced here.
Read the work in an available edition and record its title, publisher and date. Notice who is speaking, and how music changes the meaning of freedom in the scene.
In your own words, answer: What can art express that ordinary speech cannot? Does the musician seek escape, belonging, or both?
These are original discussion prompts, not quotations or translations. The linked source is in Cyrillic; this recommendation does not imply that it was originally printed in Latin letters.
callout: Read first. Then describe the scene in your own words.

title: A little poetry notebook
paragraphs: This reading list pairs Kupała's poems with a recommendation to explore Kołas. The Kupała transcriptions were made for this book; the Kołas passage is not reproduced. A poet's connection with Latin-script publishing does not prove that every poem first appeared in that script.
For a historical Latin-script book, explore Kupala's Huślar (1910). Its spelling differs from this reader. Check the specific page rather than silently replacing the letters. [8]
For each new poem, keep four notes: author and title; edition; exact original lines; your own reading and response.
callout:
What does flight mean here:
escape, discovery, return, or belonging?
